/journal/acidity-the-bright-bite.body:
The word *acidity* sounds scary, but in coffee it's a compliment. It's the brightness and liveliness that makes a cup feel fresh and alive — like the snap of biting into fruit.

Different acids show up as different sensations:

- **Citric** → lemon and lime
- **Malic** → crisp green apple
- **Phosphoric** → that bright Kenyan sparkle

There's also *acetic*, which only becomes a problem (vinegary) when there's too much of it.

Now the big beginner mix-up: **sour is not bitter.** Sour usually means lively acidity, or coffee that's under-extracted. Bitter usually means over-extraction or a darker roast. They sit at opposite ends of the cup.

> Once you separate sour from bitter, half of tasting falls into place.

Don't worry about naming the exact acid. Just ask: *does this feel bright and lively, or soft and mellow?*

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** slide the Acidity control toward *Bright* or *Smooth* on your brew to capture how lively the cup felt.
*Next in the series: [Body: the weight and feel of the cup](/journal/body-the-weight-of-the-cup) →*
/journal/acidity-the-bright-bite.excerpt: Acidity is a good thing — the lively brightness that makes coffee sparkle. It's not a fault, and it isn't bitterness.
/journal/acidity-the-bright-bite.title: Acidity: the bright bite that makes coffee sing

/journal/body-the-weight-of-the-cup.body:
Close your eyes on your next sip and ignore the taste for a second. How does the coffee *feel* in your mouth? That's body — its weight and texture.

Think of a ladder from light to heavy: **watery** (thin, like tea), then **silky**, then **syrupy**, all the way up to **creamy** and full. Most cups land somewhere along it.

A few things shape body. Brew method matters most day to day: a paper filter or pour-over feels lighter and cleaner, while a French press feels heavier with a little sediment. Processing and roast play a part too.

> A quick trick: compare coffee to milk. Skim feels watery, whole milk feels fuller. Where does your cup land?

Neither end is "better." Some people love a clean, delicate cup; others want something rich to wrap around. Body is just one more thing you get to have a preference about.

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** set the Body control to *Light*, *Medium*, or *Full* to match how heavy your brew felt on the tongue.
*Next in the series: [Sweetness and balance: when a cup just clicks](/journal/sweetness-and-balance) →*
/journal/body-the-weight-of-the-cup.excerpt: Body is how coffee feels in your mouth — light and clean, or rich and heavy. Here's how to notice it.
/journal/body-the-weight-of-the-cup.title: Body: the weight and feel of the cup

/journal/brew-method-and-clarity.body:
Here's a fun experiment: brew one bean two ways and you'll swear you bought two different coffees. The method matters that much.

A rough guide to what each brings:

- **Filter / pour-over** → clarity and higher-toned, sparkling acidity
- **French press** → body and texture, a heavier, rounder cup
- **Espresso** → concentrated and intense, everything turned up

There's also **AeroPress**, which tends to be clean and forgiving — a great place to start if you're still finding your footing.

> Want bright and crisp? Reach for filter. Want rich and full? French press. Same bean, different mood.

This is why comparing cups teaches you so fast. When you change just the method and taste the difference, you learn what *clarity* and *body* actually feel like — not as words, but as sensations on your tongue.

So don't think of brew gear as fussy. Think of it as a set of dials you get to play with.

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** record the brew method on each brew, so when you taste two cups from one bean, the difference is right there in your log.
*Next in the series: [Milk drinks: how milk changes what you taste](/journal/milk-drinks-and-taste) →*
/journal/brew-method-and-clarity.excerpt: The same bean can taste like two different coffees depending on how you brew it. Here's why.
/journal/brew-method-and-clarity.title: Brew method and clarity: same bean, different cup

/journal/build-your-palate.body:
Here's the most freeing thing about tasting: a good palate isn't something you're born with. It's something you build, one cup at a time.

The recipe is simple:

- **Taste** with attention, not on autopilot
- **Note** what you find, in your own words
- **Compare** new cups to ones you remember

Writing it down is the secret sauce. Each note becomes a little memory you can come back to, and over weeks those memories link up into a map. "This is brighter than that Colombian last week" is real tasting — and it only works if you logged the Colombian.

> Use references, too. Smell a lemon, bite an apple, taste honey — then go looking for those in the cup.

Don't aim for perfect vocabulary. Aim for honest, repeated reps. The palate follows.

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** log *every* brew, even the rushed ones — each one adds to the palate memory you're quietly building.
*Next in the series: [What roast level does to taste](/journal/what-roast-level-does-to-taste) →*
/journal/build-your-palate.excerpt: A good palate isn't a gift you're born with — it's a habit. Taste, write it down, compare, repeat.
/journal/build-your-palate.title: Build your palate: taste, note, repeat

/journal/days-off-roast-why-it-matters.body:
A common myth is that coffee is best the moment it leaves the roaster. It isn't. Freshly roasted beans are full of carbon dioxide, and that gas needs a few days to escape — a process called **degassing**.

## The rough timeline

- **0-3 days:** lots of CO2; brews can taste gassy, sharp, and hard to dial in.
- **4-14 days:** the sweet spot for most filter coffees — sweetness and clarity peak.
- **3-6 weeks:** still enjoyable, slowly fading; aromatics soften.
- **Beyond:** drinkable, but the bright top notes are mostly gone.

Espresso often wants a little *more* rest than filter — many roasters suggest 7-14 days before pulling shots.

## What to do with this

Log the **roast date** (or [tap in](/for-roasters) to capture it automatically) and check the days off roast on each brew. Over a few bags you'll find *your* window for *your* gear — and that's the whole point.
/journal/days-off-roast-why-it-matters.excerpt: Coffee isn't fresh the day it's roasted — it's fresh a few days after. Here's how degassing shapes the cup.
/journal/days-off-roast-why-it-matters.title: Days off roast: why the date on the bag matters

/journal/dialing-in-pour-over.body:
The fastest way to better pour-over is to stop changing five things at once. Start from one repeatable recipe, then move a single variable per brew.

## A starting point

- **Ratio:** 15:1 — e.g. 20 g coffee to 300 g water.
- **Grind:** medium, like coarse sand.
- **Water:** just off the boil, around 94-96 C.
- **Time:** aim for 2:30-3:00 total.

## Pour structure

1. **Bloom:** 40-50 g of water, swirl, wait 30-45 seconds.
2. **Main pours:** add water in two or three steady pours to your target weight.
3. **Drawdown:** let it finish; the bed should look flat, not cratered.

## Then adjust

Tastes thin or sour? Grind **finer**. Bitter or harsh? Grind **coarser**. Change one thing, brew again, and log it — the notes are how the lesson sticks.
/journal/dialing-in-pour-over.excerpt: A simple, repeatable V60 recipe to anchor your mornings — then adjust one variable at a time.
/journal/dialing-in-pour-over.title: Dialing in pour-over: a starting recipe

/journal/dialling-in-the-four-dials.body:
Dialling in sounds like something only baristas do. It isn't. It just means making small, deliberate changes until your cup tastes the way you want it to. Anyone can do this — no special palate, no snobbery, just a willingness to taste and tweak.

This series walks through every drink type, one at a time, with a starting recipe you can save and tap next time you log a brew. But before any of that, you need the four dials.

## Your starting point

There is no single recipe here — this post is the map for the rest. Every drink in this series is controlled by the same four levers:

- **Ratio** — how much coffee (or tea, or cocoa) to how much water. The backbone of strength and balance, usually written like 1:16 (one gram of coffee to sixteen of water).
- **Grind** — how fine or coarse you grind. Finer grinds extract faster; coarser grinds slower.
- **Time** — how long water and grounds are in contact. Longer pulls out more.
- **Temperature** — hotter water extracts faster and more aggressively; cooler water is gentler.

Keep them written down for each brew. You can only learn from a change if you know what you changed.

## Dial it in

Here is the one rule that ties the whole series together. Taste your drink and ask: is it **under-extracted** or **over-extracted**?

- **Sour, sharp, thin or weak?** You haven't pulled enough out of the grounds. It's **under-extracted**. Push harder: grind **finer**, brew **hotter**, or give it **longer**.
- **Bitter, harsh, drying or hollow?** You've pulled too much out. It's **over-extracted**. Ease off: grind **coarser**, brew **cooler**, or make it **shorter**.

That's it. Sour means do more; bitter means do less. Change **one dial at a time** by a small amount, taste again, and repeat. If you move three things at once you'll never know which one helped.

## Common mistakes

- Changing several dials at once, so you can't tell what worked.
- Not weighing anything — guessing the ratio makes every cup a fresh mystery.
- Blaming the beans before you've adjusted the grind.
- Chasing perfection on day one. Dialling in is a few cups, not one.
- Forgetting that stale or very fresh (gassy) coffee behaves differently — give beans a few days off roast.

Get comfortable with these four dials and the sour/bitter rule, and the rest of this series is just applying them to each drink.

Save your house ratio as a recipe in **My Kit** and tap it next time you log a brew.

*Next: [Dialling in espresso](/journal/dialling-in-espresso) →*

## Sources

- James Hoffmann — *The World Atlas of Coffee* (extraction, the brewing variables)
- Specialty Coffee Association — Golden Cup / extraction theory
- Barista Hustle — extraction and the taste of under/over-extraction

/journal/dialling-in-the-four-dials.title: Dialling in: the four dials

/journal/home-tasting-flight.body:
Want to level up fast? Stop tasting one coffee at a time. The single best move for your palate is a side-by-side flight — your own little cupping at home.

It's easier than it sounds:

- **Brew 2-3 coffees** the same way, side by side
- **Smell first**, going from cup to cup before you sip
- **Slurp** to spray the coffee across your whole palate

Then just compare. *Which is brighter? Which is heavier? Which finishes sweeter?* You don't need to score anything — differences pop out far more clearly than they ever do in a lone cup.

> Comparison is the great teacher. One cup tells you what it is; two cups tell you what each one *isn't*.

Try two roasts of the same origin, or two origins at the same roast. However you mix it, you'll learn more in one flight than in a week of solo cups.

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** log each cup in your flight as its own brew, then compare them side by side to see your tasting notes line up.
*Start the series: [How to taste your coffee — without the snobbery](/journal/how-to-taste-your-coffee) →*
/journal/home-tasting-flight.excerpt: The fastest way to grow your palate: taste two or three coffees side by side and let the differences teach you.
/journal/home-tasting-flight.title: A home tasting flight: set up your own cupping

/journal/how-processing-shapes-the-cup.body:
Before a bean is roasted, it goes through *processing* — how the fruit is removed from the seed after picking. It quietly shapes flavour more than most beginners expect.

The main styles, in plain terms:

- **Washed** → clean and bright, letting the bean's own character shine
- **Natural** → fruity and heavy, dried with the fruit still on
- **Honey** → in between washed and natural, often sweet and round

There's also **anaerobic**, fermented in sealed tanks, which tends to taste funky and intense — a wild ride if you're feeling adventurous.

> If a coffee tastes surprisingly fruity or even boozy, processing is often the reason.

You don't need to predict flavour from the process. It's more fun the other way around: taste the cup, then peek at how it was processed and connect the dots. Over time you'll start guessing — and being right.

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** check a bean's process on its bean page, then see if your brew matches what that style usually brings.
*Next in the series: [Tasting by origin: a quick world tour](/journal/tasting-by-origin) →*
/journal/how-processing-shapes-the-cup.excerpt: How a coffee cherry is processed after picking quietly shapes its flavour. Here's the quick guide.
/journal/how-processing-shapes-the-cup.title: How processing shapes the cup

/journal/how-to-taste-your-coffee.body:
You don't need a fancy palate to taste coffee well. You just need a little method, and the willingness to slow down for a sip.

Here's the frame coffee folks use everywhere. Five things to notice:

- **Aroma and flavour** — what you smell and taste
- **Acidity, body, sweetness** — the cup's brightness, weight, and natural sugar
- **Finish** — what lingers after you swallow

Start easy. Read the roaster's tasting notes on the bag, take a slow sip, and ask: *do I notice any of that?* You won't always, and that's fine.

> One myth worth dropping: tasting notes like "blueberry" aren't added flavourings. They describe what's naturally *there*, by association.

Taste is a skill, and skills grow with reps. The more cups you pay attention to, the more you'll notice.

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** log your next cup with [the diary walkthrough](/diary) and jot one thing you noticed in the brew note.
*Next in the series: [Smell first: why aroma is most of flavour](/journal/smell-first-aroma-and-flavour) →*
/journal/how-to-taste-your-coffee.excerpt: Tasting coffee isn't a club you have to earn into. With one simple method, anyone can notice more in the cup.
/journal/how-to-taste-your-coffee.title: How to taste your coffee — without the snobbery

/journal/milk-drinks-and-taste.body:
Loving a flat white doesn't make you a less serious taster. Milk drinks are their own delicious thing — and worth tasting on purpose.

Here's what milk does to the cup:

- **Adds sweetness** — that creamy, rounded softness
- **Adds body** — more weight and a velvety texture
- **Mutes acidity and delicate aromatics** — the bright, fragile notes fade back

So a coffee that sparkled black might feel cozy and mellow with milk. Neither version is "right" — they're just different experiences of the same bean.

> This is why a great espresso for milk is built to *balance through* it — bold enough that something still shines after the milk softens everything.

Tasting milk drinks teaches you something useful: how much of a coffee's brightness was carrying the cup, and how much was sweetness and body all along.

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** log your milk drinks too — a flat white or latte counts — and note what survives the milk and what gets softened.
*Next in the series: [A home tasting flight: set up your own cupping](/journal/home-tasting-flight) →*
/journal/milk-drinks-and-taste.excerpt: Milk isn't a downgrade — it changes the cup. It adds sweetness and body while softening acidity and aroma.
/journal/milk-drinks-and-taste.title: Milk drinks: how milk changes what you taste

/journal/smell-first-aroma-and-flavour.body:
Here's a secret that changes everything: most of what you experience as *flavour* is really *smell*.

Your nose works two ways. Lean over the cup and inhale — that's orthonasal smell. Then, as you sip and swallow, aromas drift up the back of your throat — that's retronasal smell. Together they do most of the heavy lifting your tongue gets credit for.

So before your next sip, just pause and smell. Don't hunt for the "right" answer. Maybe it's nutty, maybe floral, maybe something fruity you can't quite name yet.

And remember: when a bag says "jasmine" or "blueberry," nothing was added. Those notes are *associations* — aromas your brain links to things you already know.

> Naming smells is hard at first. Give yourself a starting point instead of a blank page.

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** open the brew's flavour wheel and tap a "start with a vibe" preset like *Bright & fruity* to anchor what your nose just found.
*Next in the series: [Acidity: the bright bite that makes coffee sing](/journal/acidity-the-bright-bite) →*
/journal/smell-first-aroma-and-flavour.excerpt: Most of what you call flavour is actually smell. Sniff your coffee before you sip and you'll taste far more.
/journal/smell-first-aroma-and-flavour.title: Smell first: why aroma is most of flavour

/journal/sweetness-and-balance.body:
Yes, coffee can taste sweet — and no, nobody added sugar. This is *perceived* sweetness, the natural impression of caramel, brown sugar, or ripe fruit that a well-grown, well-roasted bean gives you.

Sweetness is one of the loveliest things to chase, because it usually means the coffee was treated with care from farm to roast. Look for it as a roundness that softens any sharp edges.

Then there's **balance** — how acidity, body, and sweetness all sit together. A balanced cup doesn't have one element shouting over the others; it feels whole.

> When people say a coffee "just clicks," balance is usually what they mean.

You don't need to score it. Just notice: *is anything sticking out, or does it feel settled?* That instinct sharpens fast with practice.

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** when a cup tastes round and sweet, reach for the *Sweet & toasty* or *Rich & cocoa* vibe preset to set your flavour-wheel starting point.
*Next in the series: [The finish: what your coffee leaves behind](/journal/the-finish-aftertaste) →*
/journal/sweetness-and-balance.excerpt: Good coffee tastes sweet without any sugar added. When that sweetness sits nicely with everything else, the cup just clicks.
/journal/sweetness-and-balance.title: Sweetness and balance: when a cup just clicks

/journal/tap-in-verified-roast-dates.body:
Roast date is the single most useful fact about a bag of coffee, and it's the one most likely to go missing. **Tap in** fixes that.

## How it works

1. A roaster posts a **roast drop** — a fresh batch with its real roast date.
2. You **tap in** from the drop, which creates a bag on your shelf.
3. The verified roast date is copied across automatically — no typing, no guessing.

From then on, every brew you log against that bag shows accurate **days off roast**, and the provenance reads *Verified* instead of *Estimated*.

## Why it matters

Freshness is a fact, not a vibe. Knowing a coffee was nine days off roast when it tasted incredible — and twenty-eight when it tasted flat — is how you learn what to buy again.
/journal/tap-in-verified-roast-dates.excerpt: When a roaster drops a fresh batch, you can tap in to log it — and the exact roast date comes along for the ride.
/journal/tap-in-verified-roast-dates.title: Tap in: verified roast dates, one tap away

/journal/tasting-by-origin.body:
Where a coffee grows leaves a fingerprint in the cup. These are loose tendencies, not rules — every farm is different — but they're a fun place to start.

A gentle world tour:

- **Ethiopia** often tastes floral, fruity, and tea-like
- **Kenya** is often bright with a blackcurrant snap
- **Colombia** often lands balanced, with caramel and red fruit

A couple more for the road: **Brazil** often leans nutty and chocolatey with low acidity (a friend to milk drinks), and **Central America** — Guatemala especially — often comes through chocolatey and balanced.

> Treat "often" as a hint, not a promise. Half the joy is finding the exceptions.

Knowing these signatures makes browsing beans feel like travel. You start reading an origin on the bag and quietly wondering, *will this one fit the pattern?* Sometimes it nails it; sometimes it surprises you — and surprises are how your palate grows.

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** glance at a bean's origin before you brew, then log what you taste and see how close the regional hunch lands.
*Next in the series: [Brew method and clarity: same bean, different cup](/journal/brew-method-and-clarity) →*
/journal/tasting-by-origin.excerpt: Where coffee grows leaves a fingerprint in the cup. A gentle world tour of common origin signatures.
/journal/tasting-by-origin.title: Tasting by origin: a quick world tour

/journal/the-finish-aftertaste.body:
Tasting doesn't end when you swallow. The *finish* — the aftertaste — is what your coffee leaves behind, and it tells you a lot.

There are two simple things to judge:

- **Length** → does the flavour fade fast, or linger pleasantly?
- **Quality** → is what lingers clean and sweet, or dry and harsh?

A great cup often leaves a long, sweet, gentle trail — you're still enjoying it ten seconds later. A rougher cup might turn dry, bitter, or just vanish.

> Try this: take a sip, swallow, then wait and breathe out slowly. Pay attention to what's still hanging around.

Neither short nor long is automatically wrong, but a clean, sweet finish is usually a sign of a well-made coffee. And honestly, the finish is the most overlooked part of tasting — so noticing it instantly puts you ahead.

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** drop a quick line in the brew note about how the finish felt — *long and sweet*, or *short and dry*.
*Next in the series: [The flavour wheel, demystified](/journal/the-flavour-wheel-demystified) →*
/journal/the-finish-aftertaste.excerpt: The finish is everything you taste after you swallow. Notice how long it lasts and whether it's pleasant.
/journal/the-finish-aftertaste.title: The finish: what your coffee leaves behind

/journal/the-flavour-wheel-demystified.body:
If naming flavours feels impossible, the flavour wheel is here to help. It's a friendly map, not a quiz.

The one the pros use is the SCA/World Coffee Research flavour wheel, and the trick is to read it **center-out**: start broad, then get specific.

> Begin general, then narrow: *fruity → berry → blueberry*. You're allowed to stop at any ring.

So if all you know is "this tastes fruity," that's a perfect first step. With another sip you might land on *berry*. With another, *blueberry*. No pressure to reach the outer edge.

The wheel sorts everything into nine broad families — things like fruity, floral, sweet, nutty, and so on. Starting from those families makes the whole thing feel less like a memory test and more like following signposts.

You don't need to memorize it or recreate the artwork. You just need somewhere to start.

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** the brew log's flavour wheel groups notes into families like *Fruity*, *Floral*, and *Nutty/Cocoa* — pick a vibe preset, then drill into the specifics.
*Next in the series: [Build your palate: taste, note, repeat](/journal/build-your-palate) →*
/journal/the-flavour-wheel-demystified.excerpt: The flavour wheel isn't a test. It's a friendly map that helps you put words to what you taste.
/journal/the-flavour-wheel-demystified.title: The flavour wheel, demystified

/journal/what-roast-level-does-to-taste.body:
Roast level is one of the biggest dials on how your coffee tastes — and noticing it is an easy early win.

**Lighter roasts** keep more of the bean's origin character. Expect more acidity, more brightness, and clearer hints of fruit, flowers, or wherever it grew. The roaster steps back and lets the bean speak.

**Darker roasts** lean into the roast itself: roastier, more bittersweet, heavier in body, with less origin clarity. Think chocolate, toast, and a bolder, rounder cup.

> Neither is better. Some mornings call for a bright, juicy light roast; some call for a deep, comforting dark one.

Once you can feel the difference, you'll start choosing roast level on purpose instead of by accident. That's a genuine taste milestone — and it makes shopping for beans far less mysterious.

Notice it, name it, and your future cups get more intentional.

**Try it in Beanmarkd:** filter beans by roast level when you're browsing, and note the roast on each brew so patterns in your taste start to surface.
*Next in the series: [How processing shapes the cup](/journal/how-processing-shapes-the-cup) →*
